author: Autodesk
description: This graph uses tagging nodes to generate a field of flowers.
documentation:
## Field of Flowers

### What it does

This graph attempts to demonstrate the new compound tag system in Bifrost.  The compound tags are used to differentiate different geometry components, similar to a group.  You can use several different compounds to make these tags and set them as a geo property on a bifrost object.

* `tag_by_angle_between_vectors`
Tag elements if the angle between different vectors is within some threshold. For example, this could be used to tag points on a mesh whose normals are pointing upward, and the resulting tag weights can be passed into `scatter_points` to scatter snow just on the upward facing parts of the mesh.

* `tag_inside_geometry`
Tag elements that are contained within another geometry. For example this could be used to tag points that are inside a bounding mesh. The output weights are the signed distances from the elements to the surface of the `bounding_geometry`. Points inside will have positive distance values, and points outside will have negative distance values. Points on the surface will have zero distance values.

* `tag_randomly`
Tag random elements based on a probability weight threshold. A random number is generated for each element, and if the number is less than the specified `probability_weight`, it is tagged. 

* `tag_scope`
A diagnostic compound for visualizing and analyzing tagged elements of a geometry.

* `set_component_tag`
Creates a named component tag on a geometric object and assigns its members.

* `get_component_tag`
Gets the component tag data for a specific component tag.

* `interpret_auto_port_as_component_tag`
Converts various inputs into type `array<bool>` and `array<long>`. This utility node lets you build reusable compounds that support multiple input types to select points or other components on a geometry to operate on. For example, you can use it to specify which points to delete in a `delete_points` compound.

### Inputs and outputs
The input for this graph is a simple plane displacement as a "ground plane" for the flowers.

### How it works
Points are scattered on the ground plane and strands are created from these points. 

Once we have the strands, `tag_strand_ends` is used to tag and trim a random number of points at the end of each strand. 

Then, again using the `tag_strand_ends` we apply a curl to the strands - by getting the start points of each strand and using the weights output of the compound, we can curl the ends of the strands more than the beginnings of them.

`tag_strand_ends` is then used again to get the start point and start point tangent of each strand, allowing us to place a cylinder at the base of each strand that will become our "stalk"

We then get the last point (the tip) of each strand and place a pre-made flower at the end of each strand, we use `tag_strand_ends` again to retrieve the position and orientation of the last point in each strand.

Inside the compound that makes the flowers, we use several strand nodes to generate petals, florets and other parts of the flower.

Finally, the existing tags we have setup throughout the example are used to color the various parts of the flower, after the geometry has been merged.

_notes.text:
# Field of Flowers

***This graph generates a field of flowers. The steps are:***
1. Generate a ground plane and scatter points along it.
2. Generate strands at each point. These will be the stems of the flowers.
3. Trim a random number of points from the tops of each strand to give the flowers different lengths.
4. Add a bit of curl noise to the strands to make them look more natural.
4. Place cylinders at the roots of the strands and extrude them along each strand. This gives the stems some thickness.
5. Place flowers at the tips of each strand.
6. Add point colors to each part of the merged flower mesh.

Each step has some terminal outputs that one can use to inspect the result for that step.

## Setting up the Extrusion

This section is the beginning of turning our strand stalks into meshes.  We will be putting a cylinder at the base of each stalk, then extruding the top faces of that cylinder up to make a long, thin, stalk.

## Doing the Extrusion

This section performs the extrusion on the top faces of the cylinders.  The result of this is the stalk as a mesh.

## Strand Generation

Inside the *generate_strands* compound points are scattered on the terrain mesh (using *scatter_points*), then strands are generated on each point. These will become the stalks for the flowers, so **the strands need to have enough points in them to support a curve** this is achieved through the *strand_resolution* input on *create_strands_from_end_points* inside the compound).

## Strand Trim

This section will trim the top of the strands using the ***tag_strands_data*** compound and a random array.  It will select a random number of points from the end of the strands object and feed their indices into a ***delete_points*** compound.

## Curl the Strands

In this section, we will apply a curl noise to the strands that is stronger at the top of the "stalk" than the bottom.

## Adding the Flowers

Using the position and orientation of the strand ends, this section adds a flower head to each strand.

## Flower Shading and Output

Each part of the mesh was tagged in previous steps. inside the ***set_colors*** compound, those tags are used to color the flower heads.

_backdrops.title: Trim the tops of the strands by a random amount
Place some cylinders at the base of each strand
Extrude the cylinders along the strands

_notes.text: Create a simple terrain by displacement
We set unique colors to each part of the mesh using get_component_tag. (Flowers, stems, florets, etc.)
Using ***resample_strands*** to add divisions to the strands based on the *strand_resolution* input
An ***interpret_auto_port_as_component_tag*** will convert incoming data into a boolean or long array as well as indicating if the input has any data.

Here we use the ***tag_strand_ends*** component tag to get a random number of points at the end of a strand .. we're going to remove those points to get a more natural and random height distribution of the flowers.

_backdrops.title: Select a random number of points from the ends of each strand

_notes.text: In this ***tag_strand_ends*** compound, we are getting the points at the **start** of each strand, rather than the ends.  By using the weights output and the *point_ratio* selection mode, we are outputting the point ratio of the strand.  This gives us a 0-1 value for each strand that we can use to control the blending of the curl noise above.

_backdrops.title: Dampen the noise closer to the root of the strand

_notes.text: By taking a ***curl_noise*** and adding it back onto the point positions we generate an input-based noise for the stalks.

By multiplying the curl noise by <<1,0,1>> we remove any y-axis noise and then we are doing a linear interpolation with the original point positions to blend between the most curly and no curly at all.

In this section, a orientation is calculated by a ***rotation_between_vectors*** compound then the positions are sent to a loop as transforms, where a cylinder is added to the bottom most point in each strand.

The ***tag_strand_ends*** is being used to get the start point of every strand, as that is where we are going to place the cylinder that will become our "stalk".  ***update_strands_basis*** is used to get the strand's tangent vector to be used in making an orientation for these cylinders.

_backdrops.title: Select the root point of each strand, and get its position and tangent
Place cylinders at each root point

_notes.text: Merging the array from the loop, we get the indices and set a component tag (**point_stem**) on the mesh.  This allows us to retrieve them later.
Using ***filter_strands*** we get each strand in the strand object and use it as an extrusion path for the top faces of each cylinder in this loop.

_backdrops.title: Extrude each cylinder along the strand

_notes.text: By getting the length of the strand, we can calculate a scale for each flower head, based on how long the stalk strand is.
We take the position, the orientation and the scale of each flowerhead and construct an array of transform matrices.  We then transform random variations of the flower according to thous matrix

First we update the basis vectors on the strand.  Then we use the ***tag_strands_ends*** to get the very last point in each strand.  We use this point to get the position of the point for flower placement and the tangent of this last point for the direction of the flower.

_backdrops.title: Select the tip of each strand, and get its position and tangent
Scale the flower according to the stem length
Generate a few variations of the flower
Place the flowers at the tips of each stem

_notes.text:
# Create Bulb
Create and flatten the base sphere

Use the ***tag_by_angle_between_vectors*** compound to determine the angles between the face normal and an up-axis. By carefully adjusting the *max_angle* you can select only the faces at the top of the sphere.

# Prepare Base
We use ***tag_by_angles_between_vectors*** to select and use faces in the center of the flower.

_backdrops.title: Select the faces at the top of the sphere
Create a small subset of the base for scatter Points

_notes.text:
The two tag nodes selects two sets of faces based on the angle between their face normal and the up-axis. The first node uses a larger angle threshold than the second. This makes the first set of tagged faces a super set of the second set.

The difference of the two sets is a single ring of faces. Use the tag_scope to see the result.

Use the ***tag_by_angle_between_vectors*** node to determine the angles between the point normal and the up-axis. Then use these angles as weights for tag_randomly. The points with a larger weight will be more likely to be selected. This will generate a loose selection of outer points to be tagged as outside florets. The remainder will be tagged as inside florets.
Inside these compounds the geometry tags for inside and outside florets are set.

# Create Petals
In this section we use ***tag_by_angle_between_vectors*** to select faces along the edge of the flower center.  We then utilize ***set_component_tag*** to place a petal shape on each face

# Create Florets
In this section we use ***tag_by_angle_between_vectors*** and ***tag_randomly*** to create small floret in the center of the flower.

_backdrops.title: Create small florets in the middle
Determine which points should be considered inner/outer florets
Generate a ring of faces from the base sphere
Generate the flower petal shape from a sphere and place them along the face centers
Tag the inside and outside florets

_notes.text: Using ***get_geo_component*** and a ***set_component_tag*** we set a *"point_petal"* tag for use later

_backdrops.title: Randomly pick one variation of the flower to place
